# click Versus argparse

**Decision.** Ship **both**, on comparable problems, in the same repository — and say that the
comparison is the point.

**Date.** 2026-07-25, [[python-programming-laboratories]].

> "**`click` against `argparse`.** This lab uses `click`; the core CLI in `weblog.cli` uses
> `argparse`. Comparing the two on the same kind of problem is the point — `click`'s decorators are
> terser for flag soup, `argparse`'s subparsers give more control over a command hierarchy."
> — Python-Programming-Laboratories/labs/09_dataset_reports/README.md, 2026-07-25

## The split, and why it is not arbitrary

| | `weblog.cli` core | `labs/09_dataset_reports` |
|---|---|---|
| Library | [[argparse]] | [[click]] |
| Shape | multi-command hierarchy over one parsed log | one command with many flags |
| Dependency | stdlib | optional `labs` extra |

The core has to be stdlib. `pyproject.toml` declares `dependencies = []`, so any parser requiring an
install was excluded before the ergonomics were weighed at all — see
[[setuptools-and-pyproject]] and [[zero-dependency-no-build-step]]. Lab 09 sits inside the extras, so
the constraint does not bind there and click can be chosen on its merits.

That makes this a **genuinely constrained choice in one place and a free one in the other**, which is
what makes the comparison informative rather than a preference.

## The trade-off as stated

- **click** — decorators sit on the handler, so declaration and implementation cannot drift; type
  conversion and existence checks are declarative; terser when a command has many flags.
- **argparse** — subparsers give finer control over a command *hierarchy*: per-command option sets,
  per-command help, and no framework between `sys.argv` and the function. Stdlib.

## Why it is filed as a decision, not a preference

No winner is declared. The decision is to **keep both implementations rather than converge**, which
costs a reader two APIs to follow and buys a comparison that can actually be run. It is the same move
as [[keep-the-teaching-version]] and the same instinct as
[[dual-implementation-as-cross-check]] and [[multiple-solutions-side-by-side]].
